title: Reading literature and poetry
objectives: I can read short literary excerpts by Gonçalves Dias, Machado de Assis, Castro Alves and Álvares de Azevedo and follow their meaning.
I can explain why the words of literary texts are written, accented and pronounced as they are, using the stress and spelling rules.
I can recognize literary forms such as the simple pluperfect, mesoclisis, inverted word order and an adjective placed before its noun.
I can recognize and name figures of speech such as metaphor, simile, irony, personification and hyperbole.
I can use context, word families, prefixes and suffixes to work out unfamiliar words, and interpret diminutives and augmentatives.

vocabulary.note: Said e-ZI-lyu. The stress is on the third to last syllable, because the final io counts as two vowels, so no ending predicts it and the acute is written. The x in the prefix ex- before a vowel is z, as in exame and exato.

example.pt: O poeta escreveu esses versos durante o exílio.
example.en: The poet wrote these verses during his exile.
example.literal: The poet wrote these verses during the exile.

vocabulary.note: Said sow-DA-ji. Au is the diphthong ow of cow, and d before the final e (said i) is j. The stress is on da, the default for a final e, so no accent is written. No single English word covers it: it is longing for a person, a place or a time that is absent, with warmth and some sadness. The word is traced to Latin solitas, solitude. To miss someone is sentir saudade de, literally to feel longing of.

example.pt: A saudade da terra natal acompanhava o poeta.
example.en: Longing for his homeland accompanied the poet.
example.literal: The longing of-the land native accompanied the poet.

vocabulary.note: Said gor-zhe-AR. J is always the zh sound, and the infinitive ends in r, so the last syllable is stressed and no accent is written. Verbs in -ear insert an i in the forms stressed on the stem: gorjeio, gorjeia, gorjeiam, but gorjeamos. A literary verb for birdsong; the everyday verb is cantar.

example.pt: Os pássaros gorjeiam ao amanhecer.
example.en: The birds warble at dawn.

vocabulary.note: Said VAR-zya. The final ea counts as two vowels, so the stress is on the third to last syllable and the acute is written on the open a. The z starts its syllable, so it is the plain z sound.

example.pt: As várzeas ficam verdes depois da chuva.
example.en: The meadows turn green after the rain.
example.literal: The floodplains stay green after of-the rain.

vocabulary.note: Said BOS-ki. Qu before e keeps the k sound and the u is silent, and the final e is said i. The s ends its syllable before the k sound of qu, a voiceless consonant (one said without a buzz in the throat), so it is s (sh in Rio de Janeiro). The stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for a final e.

example.pt: Passeamos no bosque ao fim da tarde.
example.en: We strolled in the grove at the end of the afternoon.

vocabulary.note: Said siz-MAR. Ci is s, and the s ends its syllable before the voiced consonant m (one said with a buzz in the throat), so it is z. The infinitive ends in r, so the last syllable is stressed and no accent is written. A literary verb for thinking long and uneasily, often followed by em or com.

example.pt: Ele passava as noites cismando à janela.
example.en: He spent his nights brooding at the window.
example.literal: He spent the nights brooding at-the window.

vocabulary.note: Said pri-MOR. The word ends in r, so the last syllable is stressed by default and no accent is written. The plural primores (pri-MO-res) is stressed on the same syllable, because es defaults to the second to last, so it needs no accent either. Used of anything made with great care; the poem says os primores for the fine things of home.

example.pt: O bordado era um primor de delicadeza.
example.en: The embroidery was a masterpiece of delicacy.

vocabulary.note: Said sa-bi-AH. The word ends in a, which predicts stress on the second to last syllable, but the stress is on the last, so the acute is written, and it shows an open a. Without the accent, sabia is the imperfect of saber, said sa-BI-a. The sabiá-laranjeira, a songbird, is the national bird of Brazil. The poem writes the name with a capital letter.

example.pt: O sabiá canta na mangueira do quintal.
example.en: The thrush sings in the mango tree in the yard.

vocabulary.note: Said paw-MAY-ra. L at the end of a syllable is said w. Ei is the diphthong of English day, one beat, and it carries the default stress on the second to last syllable. Built from palma, palm, plus -eira, the suffix for a tree that bears something (compare mangueira, from manga).

example.pt: Uma palmeira alta cobria a casa de sombra.
example.en: A tall palm tree covered the house in shade.
example.literal: A palm-tree tall covered the house of shade.

vocabulary.note: Said pen-DAO, with a nasal a. En before d marks a nasal vowel, so the n is not said as a consonant. The ending ão defaults to the last syllable, so only the tilde is written. The plural is pendões. A literary word for a flag; the everyday word is bandeira.

example.pt: O pendão verde e amarelo balançava ao vento.
example.en: The green and yellow banner swayed in the wind.
example.literal: The banner green and yellow swayed at-the wind.

vocabulary.note: Said ho-ER. The initial r is the strong r, and the infinitive ends in r, so the last syllable is stressed. The o and e are two strong vowels, so they are two syllables, as in po-e-ta. Irregular: eu roo, ele rói, nós roemos, eles roem; preterite roeu; participle roído. Rói has an open stressed diphthong at the end of a word, so it takes the acute (like herói). Roído has a stressed i alone in its syllable after o, so the acute keeps the two vowels apart. Roeu has a closed e, like comeu, so it needs no accent, unlike céu. The example is a traditional tongue twister that practises the strong r.

example.pt: O rato roeu a roupa do rei de Roma.
example.en: The mouse gnawed the clothes of the king of Rome.

vocabulary.note: Said KAM-pa, with a nasal a. M before p marks a nasal vowel, and m is the letter written before p and b. The word ends in a, so the stress is on the second to last syllable and no accent is written. A literary word; everyday speech says túmulo.

example.pt: Deixaram flores sobre a campa do poeta.
example.en: They left flowers on the poet's gravestone.

vocabulary.note: Said BER-su. The cedilla makes ç the s sound before o, where c alone would be k; ç never starts a word. The stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for a final o. Figuratively, the place where something began.

example.pt: Aquela cidade foi o berço do samba.
example.en: That city was the cradle of samba.

vocabulary.note: Said de-FUN-tu with a nasal u, and in relaxed speech ji-FUN-tu, because an unstressed first e is said i and d before the i sound is j. Un before t is a nasal vowel, so the n is not said as a consonant. The stress is on the second to last syllable, so no accent is written. The everyday word is morto.

example.pt: O narrador do romance é um defunto que conta a própria vida.
example.en: The narrator of the novel is a dead man who tells his own life.
example.literal: The narrator of-the novel is a dead-man that tells the own life.

vocabulary.note: Said e-zi-TAR. The h is silent and is kept only because the Latin source had it. The s between vowels is z, and the infinitive ends in r, so the last syllable is stressed and no accent is written. It takes em before a verb (hesitar em responder) and se before a clause (hesitar se devia).

example.pt: Ela hesitou antes de abrir a carta.
example.en: She hesitated before opening the letter.

vocabulary.note: Said LA-gri-ma. The stress is on the third to last syllable, so the acute is written on the open a. G before r is the hard g, because the next letter is r and not e or i, and gr stays together in one syllable (lá-gri-ma).

example.pt: Uma lágrima escorreu pelo rosto dela.
example.en: A tear ran down her face.
example.literal: A tear dripped by-the face of-her.

vocabulary.note: Said PAW-pe-bra. The stress is on the third to last syllable, so the acute is written. The l before p ends its syllable, so it is said w, and bra is b plus the tap r in one syllable.

example.pt: O cansaço pesava sobre as pálpebras.
example.en: Tiredness weighed on his eyelids.
example.literal: The tiredness weighed on the eyelids.

vocabulary.note: Said VER-su. The s after the consonant r is s, not z, because z is the sound of a single s only between vowels. The stress is on the second to last syllable, so no accent is written. The same word also means the back of a page.

example.pt: O último verso do poema é o mais famoso.
example.en: The last line of the poem is the most famous.

vocabulary.note: Said es-TRO-fi. Greek ph is written f in Portuguese, and the final e is said i. The stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for a final e, so no accent is written.

example.pt: Cada estrofe desse poema tem quatro versos.
example.en: Each stanza of this poem has four lines.

vocabulary.note: Said HEE-ma. The initial r is the strong r, like the h of English hat. The stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for a final a, so no accent is written.

example.pt: A rima entre céu e véu é muito comum.
example.en: The rhyme between céu and véu is very common.

vocabulary.note: Eu is the pronoun I used as a noun with an article, as English can say the I. Lírico is said LI-ri-ku and is stressed on the third to last syllable, so the acute is written; Greek y is written i in Portuguese. The lyrical speaker is the voice that speaks in a poem, which is not necessarily the poet.

example.pt: O eu lírico sente saudade da pátria.
example.en: The lyrical speaker misses his homeland.
example.literal: The I lyrical feels longing of-the homeland.

vocabulary.note: Said me-TA-fo-ra. The stress is on the third to last syllable, so the acute is written. Greek ph is written f, as in estrofe. The Greek source means transfer: a metaphor transfers the name of one thing to another.

example.pt: Dizer que a vida é um rio é uma metáfora.
example.en: Saying that life is a river is a metaphor.

vocabulary.note: Said kom-pa-ra-SAO, with nasal vowels. M before p marks a nasal vowel, and ç is s before a. The ending ão defaults to the last syllable, so only the tilde is written. The ending -ção corresponds to English -tion, and the plural is comparações. In literary analysis the word names the figure that English calls a simile.

example.pt: Na comparação, o amor é como uma chama.
example.en: In the simile, love is like a flame.

vocabulary.note: Said per-so-ni-fi-ka-SAO. The word shows both spellings of the sound pair: c before a is k (fica) and ç before a is s (ção). The plural is personificações.

example.pt: A personificação dá vida ao vento no poema.
example.en: Personification gives life to the wind in the poem.

vocabulary.note: Said i-PER-bo-li. The h is silent, kept from the Greek source. The stress is on the third to last syllable, so the acute is written on the open e, and the final e is said i.

example.pt: Dizer que esperou mil anos é uma hipérbole.
example.en: Saying that one waited a thousand years is a hyperbole.

vocabulary.note: Said i-ro-NEE-a. The stress is on the i before the final a, which is the second to last syllable, the default for a final a, so no accent is written. Compare história, stressed one syllable earlier, which needs the acute.

example.pt: A ironia de Machado de Assis é sempre elegante.
example.en: Machado de Assis's irony is always elegant.

dialogues.title: Aula sobre a Canção do exílio
dialogues.context: In a literature class, Professor Marta and two students discuss the poem Canção do exílio by Gonçalves Dias.

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.pt: Hoje vamos ler a Canção do exílio, de Gonçalves Dias. Alguém sabe quando ela foi escrita?
lines.en: Today we are going to read the Canção do exílio by Gonçalves Dias. Does anyone know when it was written?
lines.literal: Today we-go to-read the Song of-the exile, of Gonçalves Dias. Someone knows when she was written?

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Em mil oitocentos e quarenta e três, professora. O poeta estava em Portugal, longe do Brasil.
lines.en: In 1843, professor. The poet was in Portugal, far from Brazil.
lines.literal: In thousand eight-hundred and forty and three, professor. The poet was in Portugal, far of-the Brazil.

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.pt: Isso mesmo. E o que o poema revela sobre o sentimento dele?
lines.en: Exactly. And what does the poem reveal about his feelings?
lines.literal: This same. And what the poem reveals about the feeling of-him?

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: Muita saudade. Ele compara a terra dele com o lugar onde está e diz que lá tudo é melhor.
lines.en: A lot of longing. He compares his land with the place where he is and says that everything there is better.
lines.literal: Much longing. He compares the land of-him with the place where he-is and says that there everything is better.

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.pt: Muito bem. Reparem que ele não diz o nome do país. Fala só de palmeiras e do sabiá.
lines.en: Very good. Notice that he does not say the name of the country. He speaks only of palm trees and the thrush.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Então as palmeiras e o sabiá são símbolos da pátria?
lines.en: So the palm trees and the thrush are symbols of the homeland?

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.pt: Exatamente. Reparem também nos versos curtos e no ritmo, que lembram uma canção.
lines.en: Exactly. Notice also the short lines and the rhythm, which remind us of a song.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: No fim ele pede a Deus que não o deixe morrer sem voltar para lá.
lines.en: At the end he asks God not to let him die without going back there.
lines.literal: At-the end he asks to God that not him let die without to-return to there.

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.pt: Sim, e nesse momento o tom muda. Da comparação alegre passamos ao desejo profundo de voltar.
lines.en: Yes, and at that moment the tone changes. From the cheerful comparison we move to the deep wish to return.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Dá para ver por que tanta gente ainda cita esse poema.
lines.en: You can see why so many people still quote this poem.
lines.literal: Gives for to-see why so-much people still quotes this poem.

dialogues.title: Clube do livro
dialogues.context: Three friends at a book club discuss Machado de Assis, the master of irony in Brazilian literature.

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: Terminei Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas. O narrador já começa dizendo que é um defunto autor!
lines.en: I finished Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas. The narrator starts right away by saying he is a dead author!
lines.literal: I-finished Memoirs Posthumous of Brás Cubas. The narrator already begins saying that he-is a dead-man author!

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.pt: É o que mais me diverte. Ele conta a própria vida depois de morto e ainda faz piada com isso.
lines.en: That is what amuses me most. He tells his own life story after dying and even jokes about it.
lines.literal: It-is the that more me amuses. He tells the own life after of dead and still makes joke with that.

lines.speaker: Zélia
lines.pt: Isso é ironia pura. Machado nunca diz as coisas diretamente. Ele deixa o leitor concluir.
lines.en: That is pure irony. Machado never says things directly. He lets the reader conclude.

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: Verdade. Na dedicatória, ele oferece o livro ao verme que roeu as frias carnes do cadáver.
lines.en: True. In the dedication, he offers the book to the worm that gnawed the cold flesh of his corpse.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.pt: Eu ri alto. É macabro, mas é engraçado. Era muito ousado para a época.
lines.en: I laughed out loud. It is macabre, but funny. It was very daring for its time.

lines.speaker: Zélia
lines.pt: Já em Dom Casmurro o tom muda. O narrador parece simpático, mas a gente começa a desconfiar dele.
lines.en: In Dom Casmurro, by contrast, the tone changes. The narrator seems likable, but we start to distrust him.
lines.literal: Already in Dom Casmurro the tone changes. The narrator seems nice, but the people begins to dis-trust of-him.

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: Será que a Capitu traiu mesmo o Bentinho? Até hoje os leitores discutem isso.
lines.en: Did Capitu really betray Bentinho, I wonder? To this day readers argue about it.
lines.literal: Will-be that the Capitu betrayed really the Bentinho? Until today the readers argue this.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.pt: Eu acho que não. Ele tinha ciúme de tudo, e talvez tudo fosse imaginação dele.
lines.en: I think not. He was jealous of everything, and perhaps everything was his imagination.
lines.literal: I think that no. He had jealousy of everything, and perhaps everything was imagination of-him.

lines.speaker: Zélia
lines.pt: Essa é a graça. Machado escreveu o livro de modo que ninguém chegasse a uma certeza.
lines.en: That is the beauty of it. Machado wrote the book so that nobody could reach certainty.
lines.literal: That is the grace. Machado wrote the book of way that nobody arrived at a certainty.

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: Vou reler com outros olhos. Me empresta a sua edição, Caio?
lines.en: I am going to reread it with fresh eyes. Will you lend me your edition, Caio?
lines.literal: I-go to-re-read with other eyes. Me lends the your edition, Caio?

dialogues.title: Oficina de escrita
dialogues.context: Carla shows a short story about her grandmother's house to her friend Paulo, who asks about her many diminutives.

lines.speaker: Carla
lines.pt: Paulo, escrevi um conto sobre a casa da minha avó. Quer ler?
lines.en: Paulo, I wrote a short story about my grandmother's house. Do you want to read it?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Claro! Mas por que você usa tantos diminutivos? Casinha, ruazinha, fogãozinho.
lines.en: Sure! But why do you use so many diminutives? Casinha, ruazinha, fogãozinho.

lines.speaker: Carla
lines.pt: É de propósito. O diminutivo mostra carinho, não apenas tamanho.
lines.en: It is on purpose. The diminutive shows affection, not just size.
lines.literal: It-is of purpose. The diminutive shows affection, not only size.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Entendi. E o cachorrão do quintal? Esse já é o contrário.
lines.en: I see. And the big dog in the yard? That one is the opposite.
lines.literal: I-understood. And the big-dog of-the yard? This-one already is the opposite.

lines.speaker: Carla
lines.pt: Isso. O aumentativo dá ideia de algo grande, mas aqui também é afetuoso. Ele era enorme e preguiçoso.
lines.en: Right. The augmentative suggests something big, but here it is affectionate too. He was huge and lazy.
lines.literal: That. The augmentative gives idea of something big, but here also it-is affectionate. He was enormous and lazy.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Deu vontade de comer pão de queijo com um cafezinho.
lines.en: It made me want to eat cheese bread with a coffee.
lines.literal: It-gave wish of to-eat bread of cheese with a little-coffee.

lines.speaker: Carla
lines.pt: É o efeito que eu queria! Tem uma frase de que eu gosto muito: a saudade, essa sim, continuava enorme.
lines.en: That is the effect I wanted! There is a sentence I like a lot: the longing, that one at least, remained enormous.
lines.literal: It-is the effect that I wanted! Has a sentence of which I like much: the longing, that-one yes, continued enormous.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Essa frase ficou ótima. Dá para sentir que você escreveu com o coração.
lines.en: That sentence turned out great. You can feel that you wrote it with your heart.
lines.literal: That sentence stayed great. Gives for to-feel that you wrote with the heart.

lines.speaker: Carla
lines.pt: Obrigada. Vou mandar o texto para um concurso de contos.
lines.en: Thank you. I am going to send the text to a short story contest.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Boa sorte! E não esqueça de me dedicar o livro quando ficar famosa.
lines.en: Good luck! And don't forget to dedicate the book to me when you become famous.
lines.literal: Good luck! And not forget of me to-dedicate the book when you-stay famous.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: stress and accents in the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Every accent mark in this unit follows from one design principle, taught in the stress lesson. Portuguese spelling lets the last letters of a word predict which syllable is stressed, and a written accent appears only where a word breaks that prediction. An accent is therefore never decoration: it says that this word is an exception to its ending, and it sits on the stressed vowel. The procedure never changes. Divide the word into syllables, find the stressed syllable by ear, read the default from the ending, and compare. Endings in a, e, o, am, em (with or without a final s) default to the second to last syllable; endings in i, u, l, r, z, ão, ã, ei, ou and similar default to the last syllable; stress on the third to last syllable has no default and is always marked.

The words of literary analysis are mostly learned words from Greek and Latin, and these tend to be stressed on the third to last syllable, so they are nearly all accented: metáfora, hipérbole, lírico, época, método, cadáver, póstumas. This is also why a cognate (a word with the same ancestor in both languages) can be said differently: English metaphor is stressed on the first syllable, Portuguese metáfora on the second, and the accent shows where. Learned words in -ia, -io and -ea need one more fact. A glide is a weak i or u said quickly together with the vowel beside it. In the spelling rule a final glide plus vowel counts as two vowels, so in memórias, pátria, exílio and várzea the stress sits on the third to last syllable and the accent is written. In ironia, poria, viria and morreria the stress is on the i itself, the second to last syllable, which is what a final a predicts, so nothing is written. The conditional ending -ia is stressed and unmarked, while the noun história, stressed one syllable earlier, is marked.

The next fact concerns vowels that stand side by side. Two vowels in separate syllables are called a hiatus. Two strong vowels (a, e, o) never form a diphthong, so the two vowels of poeta, poema and roer are separate syllables and need no mark. A stressed i or u that is the only vowel of its syllable and comes right after another vowel is written í or ú, because without the mark the pair could be read as one diphthong: país, roído, saíra, ciúme. If a consonant other than s follows it in the same syllable, as in juiz and ruim, no mark is written. And the open diphthongs éu and ói take an acute when they end a word, to show the open vowel: céu, véu, rói.

Accents belong to one form of a word, so they change with the ending. Café has an acute but cafezinho has none, because the suffix moves the stress to zi, where the ending o already predicts it. Tem (he has) becomes têm (they have) and vem becomes vêm, a circumflex that differs only in writing, since the two sound the same. Pendão keeps its tilde in pendões. A grave accent appears when the preposition a fuses with the article a or as (the crase): à janela, às folhas, às cinco. The test is to swap in a masculine word: ao quintal shows that the feminine janela takes à.

The verb forms of the simple pluperfect, explained below, follow the same logic. They end in a, so the stress falls on the syllable before -ra: che-GA-ra, VI-ra, dis-SE-ra, and no accent is needed. Saíra has an accent only because of the hiatus rule above. The forms for nós are stressed on the third to last syllable, so they are always accented: faláramos.

rows: Stress on the third to last syllable
lágrima, pálpebra, hipérbole, metáfora, lírico, pássaros, própria, época, póstumas, Álvares, método
No ending predicts this stress, so the accent is always written. The acute marks the stressed vowel and shows an open a, e or o; a circumflex, as in gênero, shows a closed one.
Final glide plus vowel counts as two vowels
The stress is on the third to last syllable by the spelling rule, so the accent is written.
Stress on the i before a final a
ironia, poria, viria, morreria, diria, dir-se-ia
The i is the second to last syllable, which a final a predicts, so no accent. Compare história.
Stress on the last syllable of a word in a, e, o
sabiá, será, voltará, vovó, Brás, lá, cá, já, só, pé, três
The default for a, e, o is the second to last syllable, so stress on the last needs an accent. A stressed one-syllable word in a, e, o is also marked.
Stress on the second to last syllable of a word in l or r
The default for l and r is the last syllable, so the accent marks the exception.
A stressed i or u alone in its syllable after another vowel
The accent keeps the two vowels from reading as one diphthong. A consonant other than s after it, as in juiz, removes the need.
Two strong vowels side by side
They never form a diphthong, so each is its own syllable and no mark is needed.
Open diphthong at the end of a word
The acute on éu and ói shows the open vowel. Roeu has a closed e and takes no accent.
Accent that changes with the ending
café and cafezinho; tem and têm; vem and vêm; pendão and pendões
Each form is checked again against the default for its own ending. The tilde stays because it also marks the nasal sound.
à janela, às folhas, às cinco, à minha terra
Preposition a plus article a or as. With the masculine, ao quintal, ao verme, ao pé, there is no accent.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: letters and letter groups in the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Spelling is a code from letters to sounds, and the sound lesson gave the code. This note applies it to the new words, sorted by the rule that explains each, so that no spelling is left unexplained. Two ideas cover almost every row. First, many letters have more than one sound, and something visible in the word decides which: the letter that follows (c and g before e or i against a, o, u), the position of the letter in its syllable (l, s and r at the end of a syllable against the start), or a mark (ç). Second, a few pairs of letters are single sounds that must never be read letter by letter: ch, lh, nh, rr, ss, sc, and qu and gu before e or i.

In the respellings, capital letters mark the stressed syllable; zh is the s of English measure; sh is the sh of shoe; j is the j of jeans; h is the strong r, like the h of English hat; w is the glide at the end of English now; ny is the ny of canyon and ly is the lli of million; a vowel written with n after it, or with a tilde, is nasal.

A third point explains the words that look strange to an English reader. Many literary and scientific words reached Portuguese from Greek and Latin, and Portuguese spelling replaced the Greek letters with sound-based ones: ph became f (metáfora, estrofe) and y became i (lírico). The silent h survives only where the source word had it (hoje, hesitar, hipérbole); it never changes the sound and only records the history of the word. Finally, the final unstressed e is said i and the final unstressed o is said u, and t or d before an i sound becomes ch or j, so tarde ends in ji, saudade ends in ji, and the word de is ji.

grammar.title: The simple pluperfect: one word for had done
grammar.explanation:
Every language needs a way to say that something happened before another past moment. English uses an auxiliary and a participle: had arrived. Portuguese has two ways. The one used in speech is built the same way as English: tinha chegado, the compound pluperfect, taught in the compound tenses lesson. The other is a single word, the simple pluperfect (mais-que-perfeito simples): chegara. It is a survivor from Latin, where the same idea was one word (amaveram became amara), and it is why literary Portuguese can say in one word what ordinary Portuguese says in two. Everyday speech gave it up long ago, so you will meet it in novels, poems, newspapers, speeches and a few fixed phrases, and almost never in conversation.

The formation rests on a form you already know. Take the third person plural of the preterite and remove the final m, and you have the form for eu, você, ele and ela: falaram gives falara, comeram gives comera, partiram gives partira. The full set of endings is -ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -reis, -ram, added to the stem that remains after -ram is removed (fala-, come-, parti-). In the forms for nós and vós the stress moves back one syllable, to the third to last, and the stress rule from the first lessons then forces a written accent on the vowel before the ending: faláramos, comêramos, partíramos (acute on a and i, circumflex on a closed e). Irregular verbs need nothing new, because the irregularity is already in the preterite: foram gives fora, disseram gives dissera, fizeram gives fizera, viram gives vira, vieram gives viera, tiveram gives tivera, saíram gives saíra.

The meaning is essentially that of tinha plus participle: an event before another past event or a past moment. Ele disse que já chegara and Ele disse que já tinha chegado say the same thing, the first in a literary register and the second in an ordinary one. The simple pluperfect needs a past reference point, usually in the same sentence (disse que, quando, nunca, antes de). Two traps follow from the form. The forms for eu and for ele are identical (chegara), so the subject has to come from context, as with the imperfect. And the form differs from the preterite only by the final m: foram (they went, they were) against fora (he had gone, he had been), chegaram against chegara. The form for eles, however, is the preterite form itself, so chegaram can be either, and context decides. Fora is also the ordinary word for outside, and context separates the two. In the old wish formula quem me dera, I wish, dera is this same pluperfect of dar, kept in a fixed phrase.

Treat it as a reader's form. In your own writing one well-placed fora or dissera gives a formal or literary tone, and the compound form is always correct. Everything else in the sentence behaves normally: object pronouns follow the placement rules of the previous unit (ninguém o vira, because ninguém is a negative word and pulls the pronoun in front of the verb).

grammar.title: Literary word order: verb first, adjective first, pronouns and omissions
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese verbs carry the person in their ending (falo, fala, falam), so the subject is often unnecessary and the language can move words around for emphasis without confusion. The neutral order is the one from the first lessons: subject, verb, object, with the adjective after the noun. Literature uses the alternatives, and each has a purpose a reader can recognize.

First, the verb may come before the subject. This is called inversion: the verb takes the most prominent position and the subject trails behind, as in Se eu morresse amanhã, viria ao menos fechar meus olhos minha triste irmã, where the subject, minha triste irmã, is the last phrase of the sentence. Ordinary speech does the same with verbs of arrival and existence (Chegou uma carta, Faltam duas pessoas); literature extends it to other verbs. The verb agrees with its subject in person and number, and that agreement tells you which noun is the subject even when it comes last: viria is singular, so the subject is irmã and not olhos.

Second, the adjective may come before the noun. In ordinary Portuguese it follows the noun, where it sorts one thing from others (a carne fria, the cold meat as against the hot). Before the noun it states a quality as already known or felt, so the writer colors the noun instead of sorting it: as frias carnes, minha triste irmã. A writer who says as frias carnes is not telling you the flesh was cold as news; the adjective sets the tone. English adjectives nearly always come first, so position cannot carry this contrast in English.

Third, writers omit what the reader can supply. Nossa vida mais amores leaves out the verb tem, understood from the lines before it. Dedico leaves out eu, because the ending -o shows who is speaking. Fourth, a phrase can be moved to the front for emphasis, as in Ao verme que primeiro roeu as frias carnes do meu cadáver dedico estas memórias. To read a sentence like that, find the verb first (dedico), read its ending for the subject (eu), and then assign the remaining phrases: estas memórias is what is dedicated and ao verme is who receives it.

Pronoun position follows the written rule of the previous unit. A verb that opens its clause takes the pronoun after it (cumprimentou-me, sentou-se, recitando-me). A word that pulls the pronoun forward, such as não, ninguém, que, se or já, puts it in front of the verb (ninguém o vira, não o deixe). Mesoclisis, the pronoun inside the verb, exists only in the future and the conditional (dir-se-ia, dar-lhe-ia). Finally, the present subjunctive in a main clause is a wish: Não permita Deus que eu morra means May God not allow me to die. Putting the subject Deus after the verb is the old pattern; modern speech puts que and the subject first, as in Que Deus te abençoe.

grammar.title: Figures of speech: when words mean more than they say
grammar.explanation:
Words have a literal meaning (sentido literal), which is what they say about the world, and writers often use them in a figurative meaning (sentido figurado), saying one thing to mean another. A figure of speech (figura de linguagem) is a recognizable technique for doing this. The figures have nearly the same names in English and Portuguese, because both languages took the terms from Greek and Latin, and they work in the same way, so there is no new idea here, only new words and the way Portuguese signals each figure. The practical test is that the literal reading is false, impossible or flat: a heart is not a boat, and a river does not cry. That mismatch is the signal to look for the figure.

A metáfora identifies one thing with another and states it as fact: Meu coração é um barco. The verb ser does the work, and no word says like. The Greek source means transfer: the name of the boat is transferred to the heart. A comparação (in English, a simile) states the likeness openly, with a word such as como, tal qual, feito or the verb parecer: forte como um touro. Note that the fixed simile forte como um touro needs no tão, where English says as strong as a bull; tão ... quanto and tanto ... quanto, from the comparatives lesson, state a measured equality, as in the line about the sea and the tears below. Feito in this sense, as in duro feito pedra, is colloquial and is the participle of fazer, made.

A personificação gives a human action or feeling to something that is not human: O vento conta segredos; a brisa beija o pendão. A hipérbole exaggerates beyond what could be true, to show intensity: esperei mil anos. A ironia says the opposite of what is meant, or lets the reader see the gap between what is said and what is true. Tone and context signal it: Que simpático! said of someone who woke you at five in the morning means the reverse of nice. Machado de Assis is the master of the quieter kind, which never states the contradiction and leaves the reader to find it. Beware of simpático as a false friend: it means nice or likable, not sympathetic.

When you read a poem, ask three questions: which two things are being connected, what feeling does the connection create, and would the literal statement have the same effect. The answer to the third is almost always no, and that difference is the poetry. The voice that speaks is the eu lírico, which is the speaker created by the poem, not necessarily the poet.

grammar.title: Reading strategies: context, word families, prefixes and suffixes
grammar.explanation:
You can read a literary text without a dictionary entry for every unknown word if you use the structure of words. Portuguese and English share thousands of words from Latin, so a large part of the vocabulary arrives in recognizable form. The method has three steps, from the outside in: context, family, parts.

Start with context. Ask what part of speech the unknown word must be, which its position and ending often show: after a, o or um it is a noun; ending in -ar, -er or -ir it is probably a verb; ending in -mente it is an adverb. Then ask what the sentence needs. In Os pássaros gorjeiam no bosque, gorjeiam ends in -am, so it is a verb with os pássaros as its subject, and it names something birds do.

Next, look for the word family. Words are built from a root, the core that carries the basic meaning, plus a prefix (a piece before the root) and a suffix (a piece after it). All the words built on one root are a word family: terra gives terreno, enterrar, terrestre, aterrissar. If you know the root you can read the family. Spelling stays regular when pieces are added, which makes families easy to see: the rr of enterrar comes straight from terra.

Finally, break the word into parts. The prefix in- means not, and its form follows the next letter: im- before b and p (impossível), i- before l, m and r (ilegal, imortal, irreal), in- elsewhere (inútil). The prefix des- reverses or negates (fazer, desfazer; confiar, desconfiar), re- means again (ler, reler) and sub- means under (subterrâneo). The suffix -mente makes an adverb, like English -ly, from the feminine form of an adjective, and it removes the adjective's written accent (fácil gives facilmente, rápida gives rapidamente), because -mente keeps its own stress. The suffix -ção turns a verb into a noun for the act or its result, like English -tion (comparar, comparação). The suffix -oso means full of, like English -ous (saudade, saudoso). The suffixes -ável and -ível mean able to be (amável, possível) and always carry an acute: they end in l, which predicts stress on the last syllable, but the stress is on the second to last. The suffix -eiro or -eira names a person with a trade (padeiro) or a tree that bears something (mangueira from manga, palmeira from palma), and -al or -zal names a place planted with something (cafezal, bananal).

One warning. A similar word does not always mean the same thing. Simpático is nice, not sympathetic; in an old text uso vulgar means common usage, not rude; pretender means to intend. Always check the guess against the context.

grammar.title: Diminutives and augmentatives
grammar.explanation:
A diminutive adds a suffix to a word to say small or, more often, dear. An augmentative adds a suffix to say large or, often, impressive or unwieldy. A suffix is a piece added to the end of a word, as the previous note explained. English does this only in a few set cases (piglet, doggie, kitchenette, Johnny) and most of them cannot be applied to new words; Portuguese does it with almost any noun, and also with many adjectives, adverbs and names (bonitinho, devagarzinho, agorinha, Aninha). Size is the literal meaning, and the feeling is the real function. A casinha is seldom smaller than a house: it is a house the speaker loves or wants to speak gently about. Um cafezinho is a polite offer, not a tiny cup. Translate the feeling, not the size.

Two diminutive suffixes do the same job, and the choice depends only on how the base word ends. Both agree in gender and number with the word: casinha, livrinho. Words ending in an unstressed vowel normally drop it and add -inho or -inha: casa gives casinha, livro gives livrinho, cachorro gives cachorrinho. Words ending in a stressed vowel, a nasal or a consonant keep the whole word and add -zinho or -zinha: café gives cafezinho, pão gives pãozinho, fogão gives fogãozinho, mulher gives mulherzinha. A few words ending in an unstressed vowel after another vowel keep it and take -zinho: rua gives ruazinha and rio gives riozinho. The suffix adds a new stressed syllable, so the accent of the base word is checked again and often disappears: café has an acute, cafezinho has none, and avó gives avozinha. The tilde of pão and fogão stays, because it marks the nasal sound as well as the stress. The plural of -zinho carries the plural mark on the base word too: pão, pães, pãezinhos.

The main augmentative suffix is -ão, with -zão after the same endings that take -zinho (cafezão). It is masculine even on a feminine noun: a casa gives o casarão, with a linking r. A feminine form in -ona exists for words naming women and sometimes for things (mulherona, mesona). The meaning can be size (casarão), admiration or scorn (um medrosão, a big coward). Some augmentatives became separate words with their own meaning: sala gives salão, porta gives portão, caixa gives caixão; you recognize them by the shared root.

Brazilians use diminutives far more than English speakers, especially to soften and be polite: um minutinho, um cafezinho, um precinho, um probleminha. In literary texts diminutives build tenderness and memory, as in the dialogue above. The same suffix can also be scornful (mulherzinha, gentinha), and only the tone and context tell you which feeling is meant.

grammar.title: Small constructions in the dialogues and readings
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese often says in a fixed construction what English says with a different verb. Dar, ter, ficar and fazer appear in many such constructions, and in each of them the verb does not carry its dictionary meaning alone; the meaning belongs to the whole phrase. The sensible method is to learn the phrase as one unit and to look at the literal words, as the literal lines in this unit do, to see the logic behind it. The table collects the constructions of the dialogues and readings, with the literal reading, the natural English and the way it is used.

Two patterns deserve a comment. The future tense can express a guess about the present: será que means will it be that, and so I wonder whether. And a contrast can be built with a pronoun and sim: essa sim means that one, yes, and singles one thing out against the others, as in a saudade, essa sim, continuava enorme. In the readings you also meet old-fashioned forms that follow the same logic: suposto o uso vulgar seja, with the subjunctive after suposto, means granted that the common usage is, and uma noite destas is one of these nights, where destas is de plus estas written as one word.

culture.title: Quatro vozes da literatura brasileira
culture.text:
Brazilian literature took shape as a national project in the nineteenth century, when the young nation looked for its own voice. Gonçalves Dias (1823 to 1864) wrote the Canção do exílio in 1843 while studying in Portugal. Its first lines are so well known that Brazilians have parodied them for generations, and the national anthem itself echoes its images of stars, flowers and groves. Gonçalves Dias died in a shipwreck returning to Brazil.

Castro Alves (1847 to 1871), known as the Poet of the Slaves, used grand, dramatic verse to denounce slavery, in poems such as Navio Negreiro. Álvares de Azevedo (1831 to 1852) died at twenty and became the emblem of dark, melancholic Romantic poetry, with themes of death, solitude and lost love.

Machado de Assis (1839 to 1908) was born in Rio de Janeiro to a poor family and became the greatest Brazilian novelist. He was the first president of the Academia Brasileira de Letras, founded in 1897. His narrators, such as Brás Cubas and Bentinho, are witty and unreliable, and his irony still surprises readers today. All four authors are in the public domain in Brazil, so their works can be read and shared freely.

Old texts look different on the page, because Portuguese spelling was reformed several times, most recently by the orthographic agreement that took effect in Brazil in 2009. The first edition of Machado's novel in 1881 spelled the title Memorias Posthumas de Braz Cubas, with th and z where modern spelling writes t and s, and the texts in this unit use current spelling. Poets also shortened words to keep a line the right length: Gonçalves Dias wrote qu'inda for que ainda. Reading these authors is the best way to meet a formal, beautiful Portuguese that is far from everyday speech but still shapes how Brazilians think about language and identity.

readings.title: Canção do exílio, de Gonçalves Dias

paragraphs.pt: Minha terra tem palmeiras, onde canta o Sabiá; as aves, que aqui gorjeiam, não gorjeiam como lá.
paragraphs.en: My land has palm trees where the thrush sings; the birds that warble here do not warble as they do there.
paragraphs.literal: My land has palm-trees, where sings the Thrush; the birds, that here warble, not warble like there.

paragraphs.pt: Nosso céu tem mais estrelas, nossas várzeas têm mais flores, nossos bosques têm mais vida, nossa vida mais amores.
paragraphs.en: Our sky has more stars, our meadows have more flowers, our groves have more life, our life has more love.
paragraphs.literal: Our sky has more stars, our floodplains have more flowers, our groves have more life, our life more loves.

paragraphs.pt: Não permita Deus que eu morra, sem que eu volte para lá; sem que desfrute os primores que não encontro por cá; sem que ainda aviste as palmeiras, onde canta o Sabiá.
paragraphs.en: May God not allow me to die without my returning there, without my enjoying the delights I cannot find here, without my yet seeing the palm trees where the thrush sings.
paragraphs.literal: Not permit God that I die, without that I return to there; without that enjoy the delights that not I-find by here; without that still I-sight the palm-trees, where sings the Thrush.

questions.prompt: Where is the lyrical speaker in the poem?
choices: In his homeland, among the palm trees
Far from his homeland, missing it
On a ship at sea
In a city in Brazil
questions.explanation: The words aqui and lá, and the last stanza, show he is away and wants to return.

questions.prompt: What do the palm trees and the thrush represent?
choices: His home country, through symbols of its nature
A new country he wants to visit
A description of a forest
A warning about danger
questions.explanation: The poet never names the country; he evokes it with nature symbols.

questions.prompt: What is the central wish expressed in the last stanza?
choices: To never leave his homeland again
To travel to a new place
To write another poem
To see his homeland again before dying
questions.explanation: He asks that he not die without going back and seeing the palm trees.

questions.prompt: In the second stanza the poet says nossa vida mais amores. What effect is created?
choices: A hyperbole celebrating his homeland as richer in everything
A description of a market
An ironic criticism of Brazil
A list of flowers
questions.explanation: Repetition and the claim that everything is more abundant at home express longing and idealization. The verb tem is left out and understood.

questions.prompt: Why does the poem say sem que eu volte, with volte, and not sem que eu volto?
choices: Because volte is the preterite
Because sem que requires the subjunctive, and the return has not happened yet
Because volte is a command to the reader
Because the poet writes in the future
questions.explanation: Sem que is a conjunction that requires the subjunctive, here the present subjunctive of voltar, because the return is only wished for.

readings.title: Duas aberturas de Machado de Assis, de Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas e de Dom Casmurro

paragraphs.pt: Ao verme que primeiro roeu as frias carnes do meu cadáver dedico como saudosa lembrança estas Memórias Póstumas.
paragraphs.en: I dedicate these Posthumous Memoirs, as a fond remembrance, to the worm that first gnawed the cold flesh of my corpse.
paragraphs.literal: To-the worm that first gnawed the cold fleshes of-the my corpse I-dedicate as longing-ful remembrance these Memoirs Posthumous.

paragraphs.pt: Algum tempo hesitei se devia abrir estas memórias pelo princípio ou pelo fim, isto é, se poria em primeiro lugar o meu nascimento ou a minha morte.
paragraphs.en: For some time I hesitated whether I should open these memoirs with the beginning or with the end, that is, whether I should put my birth or my death first.
paragraphs.literal: Some time I-hesitated if I-should open these memoirs by-the beginning or by-the end, this is, if I-would-put in first place the my birth or the my death.

paragraphs.pt: Suposto o uso vulgar seja começar pelo nascimento, duas considerações me levaram a adotar diferente método:
paragraphs.en: Granted that common usage is to begin with birth, two considerations led me to adopt a different method:
paragraphs.literal: Supposed the usage common be to-begin by-the birth, two considerations me led to adopt different method:

paragraphs.pt: a primeira é que eu não sou propriamente um autor defunto, mas um defunto autor, para quem a campa foi outro berço;
paragraphs.en: the first is that I am not, strictly speaking, an author who is dead, but a dead man who is an author, for whom the grave was another cradle;
paragraphs.literal: the first is that I not am properly an author dead, but a dead-man author, for whom the grave was other cradle;

paragraphs.pt: a segunda é que o escrito ficaria assim mais galante e mais novo.
paragraphs.en: the second is that the writing would thus be more elegant and newer.
paragraphs.literal: the second is that the writing would-stay thus more gallant and more new.

paragraphs.pt: Uma noite destas, vindo da cidade para o Engenho Novo, encontrei num trem da Central um rapaz aqui do bairro, que eu conheço de vista e de chapéu.
paragraphs.en: One of these nights, coming from the city to Engenho Novo, I met on a Central train a young man from around here, whom I know by sight and by hat.
paragraphs.literal: A night of-these, coming from-the city to the Engenho Novo, I-met in-a train of-the Central a young-man here of-the neighborhood, that I know of sight and of hat.

paragraphs.pt: Cumprimentou-me, sentou-se ao pé de mim, falou da lua e dos ministros, e acabou recitando-me versos.
paragraphs.en: He greeted me, sat down next to me, spoke of the moon and the ministers, and ended up reciting verses to me.
paragraphs.literal: Greeted-me, sat-himself at-the foot of me, spoke of-the moon and of-the ministers, and ended reciting-me verses.

questions.prompt: To whom does Brás Cubas dedicate his memoirs?
choices: His family
The worm that gnawed his corpse
The reader
His wife
questions.explanation: The ironic dedication is ao verme que primeiro roeu as frias carnes do meu cadáver.

questions.prompt: What does Brás Cubas say he hesitated about?

Whether to begin with his birth or his death
Whether to write in verse

questions.prompt: What is the humor in defunto autor rather than autor defunto?
choices: He was a dead man who became an author after death
He is an author who is pretending to be dead
He is an author who writes about funerals
He is a dead author of old books
questions.explanation: The joke turns on word order: the noun comes first and the second word describes it, so he is a dead man writing, not a writer who happened to die.

questions.prompt: Where does the second passage take place?
choices: In a school

questions.explanation: The narrator meets a young man num trem da Central.

questions.prompt: Which figure of speech makes the grave another cradle, a campa foi outro berço?
choices: Simile, because como is used
Metaphor, because the grave is identified with a cradle

questions.explanation: The grave is directly identified with a cradle, with no linking word like como: it is the place where his new life as an author began.

questions.prompt: In an old text, what does uso vulgar mean?
choices: Rude usage
Common, ordinary usage
Foreign usage
Poetic usage
questions.explanation: Vulgar here keeps its older sense of belonging to the common people, so it means ordinary. It is a false friend of English vulgar.

questions.prompt: In viria ao menos fechar meus olhos minha triste irmã, why does the sister come last and what is the subject of viria?
choices: The subject is olhos; the sister is the object
The subject is irmã, placed after the verb by inversion; viria is singular and agrees with it
The subject is eu, understood

questions.explanation: Literary inversion puts the verb first and the subject last. The singular viria agrees with irmã and not with the plural olhos.

paragraphs.pt: O vento conta segredos às folhas da mangueira. A tarde, vestida de ouro, deita-se sobre o rio.

paragraphs.pt: Lá dentro havia uma mesona de madeira, onde cabiam todos os primos, e um fogãozinho a lenha que nunca se apagava.

paragraphs.pt: Quando cresci, voltei lá e encontrei a casa menor do que me lembrava. Mas o cheirinho de pão de queijo era o mesmo, e a saudade, essa sim, continuava enorme.
paragraphs.en: When I grew up, I went back and found the house smaller than I remembered. But the smell of cheese bread was the same, and the longing, that one at least, remained enormous.
paragraphs.literal: When I-grew, I-returned there and I-found the house smaller than that me remembered. But the little-smell of bread of cheese was the same, and the longing, that-one yes, continued enormous.

questions.prompt: Which line of the poem is a metaphor?

O vento conta segredos

Meu coração é um barco

questions.prompt: What do the diminutives casinha, ruazinha and fogãozinho suggest?
choices: That things are tiny
That the narrator dislikes the house
Affection and tenderness
That the house is modern
questions.explanation: In this story the diminutives express warmth more than size.

questions.prompt: What contrast does the last sentence of the prose text make?
choices: The house is smaller but the longing is enormous
The smell is different but the house is the same
The grandmother is older but the house is new
The narrator is happy but the house is empty
questions.explanation: The adult finds the house smaller, yet the saudade is still enorme.

questions.prompt: Why is the word cheirinho spelled with -inho and not -zinho?
choices: Because cheiro ends in an unstressed o, which is dropped before -inho
Because cheiro ends in a consonant
Because -zinho is only used for people
Because cheiro is a verb
questions.explanation: Words ending in an unstressed vowel drop it and take -inho (cheiro, cheirinho); words ending in a stressed vowel, a nasal or a consonant take -zinho.

exercises.prompt: Why does lágrima carry a written accent?
choices: It is stressed on the third to last syllable, and no ending predicts that
It ends in a, and every word ending in a needs an accent
The á is a nasal vowel
The accent keeps two vowels from forming a diphthong
exercises.explanation: An ending predicts stress only on the last or the second to last syllable. Stress on the third to last syllable is always written, with the acute on an open vowel.

exercises.prompt: Which spelling is the bird, stressed on the last syllable?
choices: sabia
sabiá
sabiã
sabiâ
exercises.explanation: The ending a predicts stress on the second to last syllable. The bird is stressed on the last, which breaks the default, so the acute marks it. Sabia without a mark is the imperfect of saber, stressed sa-BI-a.

exercises.prompt: Why is the cedilla written in comparação?
choices: It marks the stressed syllable
It makes the vowel nasal
It writes the s sound before a, where c alone would be k
It joins the root to the suffix
exercises.explanation: C before a, o or u is k. To write the s sound there, Portuguese uses ç. The nasal sound is written by the tilde.

exercises.prompt: Why does amável carry an accent?
choices: It ends in l, which predicts stress on the last syllable, but the stress is on the second to last
It ends in a vowel
It has a nasal vowel
It is stressed on the third to last syllable
exercises.explanation: A-MÁ-vel is stressed on the second to last syllable. The ending l predicts the last, so the exception is marked. All words in -ável and -ível carry the acute for this reason.

exercises.prompt: What separates chegaram, they arrived, from the simple pluperfect chegara, in form and meaning?
choices: Chegara has an extra accent and means the same
Chegara lacks the final m and means he had arrived
Chegara ends in -ei and means I arrived
Chegara is a command
exercises.explanation: The simple pluperfect is the preterite form for eles without its final m, and it means had arrived, like tinha chegado.

exercises.prompt: Why does Cumprimentou-me put the pronoun after the verb?
choices: Because me is always written after the verb
Because the verb is in the preterite
Because the verb opens its clause and nothing in front of it pulls the pronoun forward, so written Portuguese uses enclisis
Because me is a reflexive pronoun
exercises.explanation: Enclisis is the default in careful writing. Only an attractor such as não, que or ninguém moves the pronoun in front of the verb.

exercises.prompt: In Dir-se-ia que o rio chorava, where does the pronoun se stand, and in which tenses is that possible?
choices: After the verb, in any tense
Before the verb, in the conditional only
Inside the verb, in the future and the conditional
Inside the verb, in the preterite and the imperfect
exercises.explanation: Mesoclisis puts the pronoun between the infinitive and the ending, and exists only in the simple future and the conditional, which began as the infinitive plus a form of haver.

exercises.prompt: In nossa vida mais amores, which word is understood but left out?
choices: é
tem
faz
está
exercises.explanation: The earlier clauses have tem (nosso céu tem mais estrelas). The poet leaves it out because the reader can supply it.

exercises.prompt: Ela é bonita como uma flor. Which figure of speech is this, and what shows it?
choices: Metaphor, because she is identified with a flower
Simile, because como states the likeness openly
Personification, because a flower is given human traits
Hyperbole, because her beauty is exaggerated
exercises.explanation: A word such as como, tal qual or feito states the likeness, which makes it a comparação. A metaphor would say Ela é uma flor.

exercises.prompt: Which figure of speech is O vento conta segredos às folhas, and why?
choices: Personification: the wind does something only people do
Metaphor: the wind is identified with a person by the verb ser
Hyperbole: the wind is exaggerated
Irony: the sentence means the opposite
exercises.explanation: Telling secrets is a human action, and the sentence gives it to the wind. There is no ser that identifies the wind with a person.

exercises.prompt: Why does cafezinho have no accent although café does?
choices: The suffix makes the word nasal
The suffix moves the stress to zi, where the ending o already predicts it, so no mark is needed
Accents are never written in diminutives
Cafezinho is an unrelated word
exercises.explanation: An accent belongs to one form of a word. Ca-fe-ZI-nho is stressed on the second to last syllable, the default for a final o.

exercises.prompt: What happens to the gender of a feminine noun such as casa when the augmentative -ão is added?
choices: It becomes masculine: a casa, o casarão
It stays feminine: a casarão
It becomes plural
It becomes a verb
exercises.explanation: The augmentative -ão is masculine even on feminine nouns. A feminine augmentative exists in -ona for words naming women, as in mulherona.

exercises.hint_en: He had never seen so much beauty. Use the simple pluperfect.

exercises.hint_en: The opposite of possible is impossible.
exercises.explanation: The prefix in- means not, and it becomes im- before b and p.

exercises.prompt_pt: Há muitos ___ verdes e amarelos na praça.

exercises.explanation: The plural of pendão is pendões: the ending ão becomes ões, and the tilde stays as the mark of the nasal sound.

exercises.hint_en: He did not tell me anything.

exercises.hint_en: I will give him the answer tomorrow.
exercises.explanation: Mesoclisis puts the pronoun between the infinitive and the ending. Lhe is the indirect object to him, to her or to you.
